newsitem.title: UK: Northern Ireland awaits fateful parade decision.
newsitem.headline: Northern Ireland awaits fateful parade decision.

text.p: Northern Ireland anxiously awaited word on Saturday evening on whether a flashpoint Orange Order parade would go ahead on Sunday over the objections of Catholic Irish nationalists along its route.

Breandan Mac Cionnaith, spokesman for Catholics of the Garvaghy Road residents association who want the parade banned, told a defiant rally of 500 of his supporters that the government had told him no decision had yet been made.

"I think we are moving into a crucial phase this evening. I would ask people to be alert at this time," he told men, women and children standing shoulder to shoulder beneath Irish tricolour flags along the proposed Orange Order march route.

They held aloft placards for the encamped media saying "No talk, No Walk" and "Ban sectarian marches" while in another part of town pro-British Protestants gathered under Union Jack flags to speculate how the standoff would end.

Twenty-four hours after Mowlam urged the Orange Order to be "flexible" there was no word on whether the march would be banned, allowed or rerouted or when a decision would be made known to the province's 1.5 million people.

Speculation abounded but there was no word from police or the government's Northern Ireland office as to the timing or nature of any decision, one of the toughest to confront the British government since it came to power in May 1 elections.

Local residents, Protestants and Catholics alike, wondered if an announcement would be delayed until shortly before the march is scheduled to start at 10 a.m. (0900 GMT) on Sunday to forestall trouble from Orange Order supporters or their rivals.

British troops encircled the southern town of Portadown where rival Irish and British flags were hoisted by the polarised communities in a trial of strength that mirrored the centuries-old divisions in the province.
British Prime Minister Tony Blair, speaking in England, said the government was doing everything possible to reconcile the Orange Order and Catholic Irish nationalists.

"The real hope and possibility exist for peace. I hope that the voice of reason can be heard in Northern Ireland," said Blair, adding his voice to a chorus of appeals to avoid a repeat of last year's upheaval caused by the same parade.
A Protestant cleric urged his faithful to accept whatever decision is made and spare the province from violence.

"My prayer and my advice to the whole Orange Order is that whatever decision is taken we have got to be peaceful and lawful and this country must not be plunged into the terrors of violence and bigotry and intolerance we saw last year," Reverend William Bingham told the BBC.
Spokesmen for the Order, a religously-based pro-British organisation, refuse contact with the Garvaghy Road Catholics who say the parade is sectarian intimidation.

The Orange Order says the march is a birthright and that the road belongs to the British monarch, not to those who live beside it, and that to bow to the residents' wishes insults their religion, civil rights and British loyalties.

The dispute is hanging over Anglo-Irish efforts to give a stalemated Northern Ireland peace process a new lease of life and persuade Catholic-backed Irish Republican Army (IRA) guerrillas to call a halt to their war against British rule.

Last year the march, known as Drumcree after the small Protestant church at which the Orange Order stops for prayers, erupted into days of rioting which shut down roads, the airport and towns and caused millions of pounds (dollars) of damage.
Police at first banned the parade then bowed to Protestant rioting and let it go ahead, igniting Catholic fury instead.
